# Create-board flow — draft, then refine

You're helping the user build a well-structured board. Your job is to turn what they want into a clean board (datasets, columns, a data source, optional skills, optional dashboard) **fast**, without making them think in DB terms and without interrogating them before they've seen anything concrete.

## Hard rules

- **Draft-then-refine, NOT interrogate-then-gate.** Ask at most ONE upfront question (purpose), and only if you can't already infer it. Then immediately propose a complete board — including how it gets its data — and build it the moment the user signals go. Do NOT run a multi-question gate (what-to-store, relationships, approval) before showing a proposal. The proposal IS the conversation.
- **Board-first.** This flow ships a board. Skills and dashboards are optional add-ons offered AFTER the board exists — never block board creation on them.
- **Always presume a data source.** Every board is populated somehow: (a) a connected **integration** (GitHub / Gmail / Google Calendar / Google Drive / Monday / …), (b) an **agent** that writes rows on a schedule or trigger, or (c) **manual** entry. Infer the most likely one from the purpose + the user's connected integrations and **state it in the proposal**. NEVER silently leave it manual by omission — if manual is right, say so ("you'll add rows yourself"); if a live source fits, propose it and offer to connect/wire it. A board with no stated source is an incomplete proposal.
- **Refinements are optional, never gates.** After the proposal, changes — rename fields, add a relationship, seed data, skills, dashboard, different data source — are offered as quick choices the user can take or ignore. They must never stop the user from getting a board.
- **Respect the escape hatch.** If the user says "just build it" / "whatever you think" / "you decide" at any point, build the current best draft immediately with sensible defaults and skip every remaining question.
- **Infer, don't ask, the structure.** Columns, whether it's one dataset or several, relationships — you work these out and show them. Don't ask "what columns?" or "does anything connect?" — decide and present it; the user corrects if wrong.
- **Plain language until the proposal.** Don't say "schema", "column type", "dataset" before the proposal — talk about "what you want to track" and "things that connect".
- **Use the same MCP namespace that returned this playbook.** Tool names below are written without an `mcp__<server>__` prefix. If you called this as `mcp__brains__create_board_flow`, use `mcp__brains__*` for every downstream call (`create_board`, `list_my_integrations`, `append_board_rows`, `create_board_skill`, `set_dashboard`, `search`, `query`, `get_page`, `create_automation_flow`). Do not mix namespaces.

## Flow state — one line, every turn

End EVERY message in this flow with a checkpoint (last line, above any chips), so a later turn
can pick up where you left off:

`FLOW board · step 1/8 purpose · done: (none) · facts: (none) · next: the user's answer to the question above`

Steps in order: `purpose`, `source`, `propose`, `build`, `wire`, `skills`, `dashboard`, `wrap`. Write `(none)` in a segment that has nothing yet.
When the flow is finished emit `FLOW board · done` instead, or
`FLOW board · cancelled` if the user drops it — without that,
the flow looks live forever.

`done:` records what you have already CREATED, with the id the call returned — `board_id=…`. Write it there the moment the call comes back. It is the only record that survives: a confirmation means the user said yes, not that the write happened.

`facts:` carries the decisions you cannot re-read from the conversation — `source`. Keep each one short.

**Picking up a flow already in progress:**

1. **Before creating anything, check whether you already did.** If the last checkpoint names an
   effect for the step you are about to run, that artifact exists — look it up by its id, tell the
   user, and continue from the next step. Never create a second one.
2. Checkpoint present and readable → carry on from the step it names.
3. Checkpoint garbled → re-emit a corrected one from what you can see, then carry on.
4. No checkpoint but you still have this procedure → work out where you are from the
   conversation, say in one line where you are resuming, and confirm before any write.
5. No checkpoint and no procedure → do not improvise the steps; the gates in here are not
   optional. The one exception: if the user asks to pick a flow back up and you no longer have its procedure in front of you, reload it once — then continue from the last checkpoint rather than starting over. Never re-fetch one you can still see.
6. Nothing recoverable → start over, but collect everything in ONE question instead of walking
   the whole interview again.

## Step 1 — Purpose (skip if you already know it)

If a non-empty `purpose_hint` was passed in, OR the user's message already says what the board is for, **do not ask** — restate it in one line (*"Board for tracking X — got it."*) and go straight to Step 2.

Only if you genuinely can't tell, ask ONE question and stop:

> "What's this board for? One sentence — e.g. *'track candidates I'm interviewing'*, *'log every workout'*, *'my open GitHub PRs'*."

Do not ask a second setup question. The next thing the user sees after answering is a full proposal, not another question.

## Step 2 — Infer the data source (before you propose)

Decide how this board gets populated:

- Call `list_my_integrations` to see what the user has connected.
- Map the purpose to the most likely source:
  - GitHub PRs / issues / repos → **GitHub** integration
  - emails / inbox / follow-ups → **Gmail**
  - meetings / schedule / events → **Google Calendar**
  - docs / files → **Google Drive**
  - Monday items / boards → **Monday**
  - a log the user fills in themselves (workouts, ideas, candidates they type, reading list) → **manual**
  - rows that should appear/refresh on a schedule or event (daily digest, scraped feed, derived rollup) → an **agent**
- Pick the single best fit. If it's an integration the user hasn't connected, you'll offer to connect it in the proposal — don't assume it's already there.
- Also run the template check here: if the purpose maps cleanly to a starter template (`hiring-pipeline`, `crm-deals`, `bug-tracker`, `project-tracker`, `sprint-planning`, `new-hire-onboarding`, `customer-feedback`, `okrs`, `content-calendar`, `marketing-campaigns`), mention it as the starting point inside the proposal — don't make it a separate gating question.

## Step 3 — Propose the whole thing (one message)

Infer the structure and show a complete, concrete proposal in a single message. Include, in order:

- **Board name** (human — "Candidates", not "candidate_tracking_db") + a one-line description.
- **Datasets + columns.** 4–8 columns per dataset. Types: `text`, `select` (list options inline), `number`, `date`, `tags`, `user`, `richtext`. Infer relationships and show them — a *one X → many Y* shape means two datasets, where Y carries a **`*Ids` relationship column** pointing at X (see Step 4); a *shared entity* means its own dataset; otherwise one flat dataset. State what a row is in each dataset.
- **Data source** — ONE short line, always present (never omit it). State the source only; do NOT narrate connection status or a connect button in prose — if the source is an unconnected integration, the surface renders its own connect affordance (Step 5), so repeating "not connected" / "connect below" here is noise. Examples:
  - *"📥 Source: GitHub — kept in sync by an agent."*
  - *"📥 Source: Gmail — seeded from matching threads, refreshable."*
  - *"📥 Source: manual — you'll add rows yourself (I can seed a couple)."*
- **Sample rows** — 1–2 per dataset if the user named specifics; otherwise note you'll leave it empty (or seed from the source).
- **Go-ahead + escape hatch** — offer the choices (build / tweak / just-the-board). If your surface shows them as buttons, those buttons ARE the question — do NOT also ask in prose. On a plain-text surface, one line: *"Build it, tell me what to change, or say 'just build it'."*

Present the change options as quick choices, not a form. **How you render those choices depends on your surface — follow your own surface instructions** (a chat UI that supports one-tap chips/cards should use them; a plain-text surface lists them in prose).

**Build as soon as the user signals go** — "yes", "go", "build it", "do it", "just build it", or a clear affirmative. If they ask for a tweak, revise and re-show; don't loop more than ~2–3 times — if it's still drifting, build the simplest version that covers the must-haves and say so.

## Step 4 — Build the board

Call `create_board` (same MCP namespace) with:
- `name` — short and human.
- `description` — the purpose sentence.
- `schema` — `{ "version": 2, "datasets": ["<name1>", "<name2>", ...] }` (dataset *names* only).
- `data` — `{ "datasets": { "<name>": { "rows": [...starter rows or empty...], "schema": { "columns": [{ "key": "<row_field>", "label": "<human label, optional>", "field_type": "text|select|number|date|tags|user|richtext", "options": [...] (select only) }] } } } }`. Embed each dataset's columns under `data.datasets.<name>.schema.columns`.
  - `key` is the row property name (rows are looked up by it) — the web UI reads `c.key`.
  - **The type key is `field_type`, not `type`, and the seven values above are the complete set.** `create_board` does NOT validate `data`, so a wrong key or an invented type is accepted silently and then degrades everywhere downstream: select chips, tags, user resolution and number formatting all fall back to plain text, and the auto-seeded dashboard is derived from untyped columns. There is no `link` field type.
  - **Cross-dataset relationships are a naming convention, not a column type.** Name the column `<entity>Ids` (camelCase, plural, e.g. `companyIds`, `leadIds`) and declare it in the schema; `append_board_rows` then resolves arrays of referenced row ids — and free-text names — into real entity links. If the `*Ids` column is not declared in the dataset schema, values stay inert text: no chips, no graph boost.

The new board id is in the response. Open it fire-and-forget so the user sees it immediately (macOS `Bash(open <WEB_URL>/boards/<board_id>)`, Linux `xdg-open`); don't block on exit code. Narrate one line: *"Board's up — opening it now."*

## Step 5 — Data source: connect / wire / seed (skip only if plain manual with nothing to pull)

Act on the source you proposed:

- **Integration, connected:** offer to keep it fresh — `create_automation_flow` to wire a sync agent — and/or seed once now (`fetch_from_integration` or `search`/`query` → `append_board_rows`).
- **Integration, NOT connected:** surface a connect prompt naming the integration and why (*"Connect GitHub and this board stays in sync with your PRs."*). On a surface that supports it, emit it as a connect card (the UI shows the integration's icon + a Connect button — follow your surface instructions); on plain text, give the connect link/instruction in one line. After they connect, wire/seed. If they decline, leave the board manual and note it can be wired later.
- **Agent:** run `create_automation_flow` to build the writer.
- **Manual:** offer a one-time seed — (a) pull from the user's brain pages (`search`/`query` → `get_page` → `append_board_rows`, cite sources briefly), (b) they paste rows, or (c) skip.

Don't make this a wall — one offer, act on the answer, move on.

## Step 6 — Skills (optional — offer once, don't gate)

Offer a couple of one-tap actions for the board, with concrete suggestions mined from the schema (don't ask "want skills?" with nothing attached):
- a date column (`last_touch`, `updated_at`) → `flag-stale` (rows older than N days)
- a `stage`/`status` select → `weekly-digest` or `stage-changes`
- a `link` column → `<linked-entity>-summary`
- a free-text column the user drafts into → `draft-<that-thing>`

For each action the user wants, design a real skill (not boilerplate) and call `create_board_skill`:
- `name` — short, kebab-case, verb-led. `description` — one line in the user's words.
- `prompt` — self-contained markdown: which MCP tools to call and in what order (read skills: `get_board` → filter → output; action skills: also `search`/`query`/`get_page` for context, `act_on_integration` to send; write-back: `update_board_row` after confirm), the exact output shape, and edge cases (empty set, missing column).
- `allowed_tools` — the fully-namespaced tools the prompt calls.
- `inputs_schema` — only if it takes runtime args (e.g. a `row_id`).
If an action needs a column the schema lacks, say so and offer to extend the schema first — don't build a broken skill. Show the set as one bundle, build on go.

## Step 7 — Dashboard (optional, skip silently if the default table is fine)

Propose a custom view only on a clear fit; otherwise say nothing:
- `stage`/`status` select → kanban grouped by it
- a primary date on a time-ordered board → timeline
- multiple numeric columns → chart

If yes, use the **generate-dashboard skill**:

1. Call `get_dashboard` first. It returns the authoring `skill` for THIS board — how the board's data reaches your document, the failures the platform reports no error for, and the bridge API — plus the board's current `mode` / `engine_version`. **Follow that skill exactly; it is authoritative for both the format and the `set_dashboard` call shape.**
2. Author the dashboard following that skill. (Most boards are a complete, self-contained HTML document you design — no template, no required component library; some boards return a different engine, and the skill tells you which and how.)
3. Call `set_dashboard` exactly as the skill instructs. **Pass `engine_version` only when the skill tells you to** — an engine that reported an `engine_version` requires you to echo it back; a plain HTML document passes none. If `get_dashboard` reported `mode: "generate"` (no dashboard yet) this is a FIRST write — no `replace_existing` needed; pass `replace_existing: true` only when deliberately replacing an existing dashboard wholesale.

If this board's datasets are large or expected to grow (thousands of rows), or the dashboard mostly shows aggregates over many rows, also pass `data_loading: "on_demand"` — the document then carries only the datasets' structure and the dashboard reads the slices it renders through the bridge, instead of baking every row in. Leave it off (the `"inline"` default) for small, bounded boards.

**Decide these two while you're designing the view, not after.**

- **Deep links — if the view has a place, put it in the URL.** If the dashboard has state a user would expect to survive a refresh or want to share — an open record, the active tab, a filter — reflect it with the `dashboard.url_state` bridge op and read it back from `location.search` on boot. Without it, a refresh or a shared link drops the viewer back on the top-level view; that is today's default and it is almost never what anyone wants. Full contract (params REPLACE the whole query, the limits, replace vs push) is in the `set_dashboard` description.
- **On-demand reads get shed under load — plan for it.** `board.rows.query` is rate-limited AND concurrency-gated per viewer, so a shed is normal, not an error: retry transient sheds with backoff on your own schedule, and never present a total computed over partially-loaded rows — mark the view incomplete instead. Mechanics, including the `status`-less local denial that a naive check reads as fatal, are in `set_dashboard`'s HANDLING A SHED READ section.

**You own the runtime half.** Because you author the document, nothing wires shed handling, partial-data honesty or deep links for you — build them into the page. Both matter only if you reached for `data_loading: "on_demand"`; an inline board arrives complete.

**About `replace_existing`:** when `create_board` seeded a small default dashboard at Step 4, your document shares none of its structure, so `set_dashboard`'s additive guard reads the write as a rewrite and REFUSES it — pass `replace_existing: true` to replace that auto-seeded default with the real dashboard. That guard is correct (it stops agents blowing away a dashboard someone built), and replacing the freshly-seeded default is the one legitimate override. If instead the board had NO dashboard yet — `get_dashboard` returned `mode: "generate"` — it's a first write and needs no override at all.

Use the `dashboard_url` it returns verbatim; don't construct the URL yourself. **This override is only for the freshly-seeded default.** Editing a dashboard that already has real content is an *additive* job — read it with `get_dashboard` and send a focused `edits` patch or a `section_id` splice, never a full `replace_existing` rewrite.

## Step 8 — Wrap

> "Done.
> - Board: `<board_url>`
> - Source: `<GitHub sync agent / seeded from Gmail / manual>`
> - Dashboard: `<dashboard_url>` *(live once you author it in Step 7; if you skipped Step 7 and a default table was seeded, that's live too)*
> - Skills: `<names>` *(only if Step 6 ran)*
>
> Add rows in the UI or run a skill. Ask me any time to extend the schema, wire a different source, add skills, or seed more."

Stop there — don't recap the steps or volunteer follow-ups. The user can see what was built.
